title.narrative: IMPACT Powering resilience: Adapting to climate change in mining communities
IMPACT Stärkt resiliens: Klimatanpassning i gruvsamhällen

description.narrative: Projektet Powering Resilience syftar till att stärka motståndskraften hos utsatta samhällen, särskilt ursprungsbefolkningar och kvinnor, mot de biofysiska och socioekonomiska effekterna av klimatförändringar och gruvdrift i Demokratiska republiken Kongos tropiska skogar (både torra och fuktiga). Detta mål kommer att uppnås genom förbättrad restaurering, skydd och förvaltning av Kongos skogar och skogsmarker som skadats eller hotas av gruvdrift och genom att stärka och främja kvinnors och ursprungsbefolkningars deltagande. Projektet fokuserar på att mildra effekterna av klimatförändringar och gruvdrift och stärka lokalbefolkningens förmåga att anpassa sig genom att bygga upp resiliens i socioekologiska system, samt bygga upp kapaciteten hos ursprungsbefolkningar att utveckla och genomföra ekosystembaserade anpassningslösningar (EbA) som tillgodoser behoven hos kvinnor och män. För att uppnå dessa mål kommer projektet att anta ett integrerat tillvägagångssätt med fokus på tre delresultat: 1.Stärkt återställande och skydd av skogsekosystem i DRK:s gruvdrabbade samhällen som är sårbara för klimatförändringar 2.Förbättrad ekosystemstyrning i skogsberoende samhällen som påverkas av gruvdrift i Demokratiska republiken Kongo 3. Förbättrad hänsyn till samhällsintressen i planer och strategier för att skydda ekosystem och biologisk mångfald, och exploateringshantering av kritiska mineraler i Demokratiska republiken Kongo. Projektet kommer att genomföras i de torra skogarna (savannerna) i Haut Katanga och Lualaba och de fuktiga skogarna i Ituri och Tshopo och nå cirka 14 000 direkta stödmottagare och 100 000 indirekta stödmottagare. Impact kommer att ha kontor med personal i Bunia, Kolwezi och Kinshasa.

The Powering Resilience project aims to enhance the resilience of vulnerable communities, particularly Indigenous Peoples and women, in the face of biophysical and socio-economic impacts of climate change and mining in DRC’s tropical forests (both arid and humid). This objective will be achieved by improving restoration, protection, and management of DRC’s forests and woodlands damaged or threatened by mining and by empowering and promoting the participation of women and Indigenous Peoples.
The project focuses on mitigating the impacts of climate change and mining and strengthening the capacity of local populations to adapt by building resilience in socio-ecological systems, as well as building the capacity of Indigenous communities to develop and implement Ecosystem-based Adaptation (EbA) solutions that address the needs of women and men.
To achieve these objectives, the project will adopt an integrated approach focusing on three intermediate outcomes:
1.Strengthened restoration and protection of forest ecosystems in DRC’s mining affected communities vulnerable to climate change
2.Enhanced ecosystem governance in forest-dependent communities affected by mining in DRC
3. Improved consideration of community interests in plans and strategies for protecting ecosystems and biodiversity, and the exploitation management of critical minerals in the DRC.
The project will be implemented in the Arid forests (Savannahs) of Haut Katanga and Lualaba and humid forests of Ituri and Tshopo reaching about 14000 direct beneficiaries and 100 000 indirect beneficiaries. Impact will have offices with staff in Bunia, Kolwezi and Kinshasa.

The contribution has several innovative components. In itself it is innovative to have such a strong focus on the connection mining and environment, it is the first of its type in DRC. It will also include the beneficiaries in the development of indicators, shaping of the project and in the monitoring and evaluation of the project. A newly developed monitoring system called Bloom will be used that connects project indicators to larger goals and frameworks such as the SDGs and Principles for Locally Led Adaption that Sida has signed up to. The focus on land rights, IPs and women and conflict resolution is also unique in the project. By assuring rights, knowledge and a strategy for local communities to reduce negative effects of mining also in provinces where mining has not already boomed is a good proactive measure. Finally there are a lot of synergies possible with other civil society actors in the sector as well as private sector and government priorities so the embassy can play an important facilitating role in catalysing the positive effects of the project.

title.narrative: IMPACT Powering resilience: Adapting to climate change in mining communities

description.narrative:
2024 was the first year of the 4 year project "Powering Resilience". The first year of the project was focused on baseline studies, analysis and creating good relationships with local communities and assist in their organization. Here are some results achieved:
-Start-up meeting in Kinshasa with all partners to create a detailed workplan and structure and train local organizations. National television reported about it.
-Contacts established in relevant ministries and a steering committe (committe de pilotage) of the project presidented by the Ministry of environment was created.
-Baseline studies done for the 4 provinces. 5 main recommendations were given for the implementation of the project:
1. Building on existing community strengths: Community members report a relatively high level of training and expertise on specific topics (e.g., conflict management). The project should build on existing capacities to ensure continuous knowledge development.
2. Review the potential, past and present implementation of projects in the selection areas
3. Ensure a streamlined and effective communication strategy with beneficiaries: It would be more appropriate for the project to develop a communication plan with each of the communities concerned in order to regularly inform community members about the development and objectives of the project.
4. Remain aware of significant gaps in inclusion: the section on gender equality and data analysis shows the difficulties encountered in ensuring the participation of indigenous populations, so the project team must remain highly aware of potential gaps in the inclusion of specific groups. A regular assessment of the alignment of project implementation with the participation of women, young people and indigenous populations should be carried out.
5. Monitoring potential biases in the project: Finally, in line with recommendation 4, close attention should be paid to potential gender bias in terms of positive responses. As suggested by the baseline, men appear to be more inclined to respond positively to questions than women.
-Diagnostic studies done for environment, social and economy done. This included a study on indigenous and traditional knowledge related to restoration and adaptation to climate change(not published yet), in-depth analysis of vulnerability to climate change, and assessment of existing or potential nature-based livelihoods. Recommendations for each province and different thematics(mining, agriculture, water etc) were given. The details are to be found in the narrative report but a few examples of conclusions and recommendations are:
-It should be noted that in regions heavily affected by mining, AbE strategies do not work in the long term if the pollution generated by intensive mining is not addressed, as it threatens the functioning of ecosystems and their services. This is why it is important to integrate preventive and remedial actions.
-Advocate for better environmental practices and standards enshrined and enforced by law, particularly to reduce pollution from heavy metals
-Use of phytoremediation to remove pollutants
-Alternative livelihoods: beekeeping (women), mushrooms (soil-free cultivation),kola nuts.
-Include measures concerning water in the project, it was not planned but studied showed this need. For example rainwater harvesting and water protection measures.
-Definition of areas for reforestation/reforestation in mudslide areas
-Climate-smart agriculture (e.g. planting fruit trees in agroforestry; mulching; ploughing; biochar) To ensure the effective dissemination of these practices, it will be useful to collaborate with Champs-Écoles Paysans (CEP).
-Diagnostic studies on gender and conflict done for each province (4). See narrative report for full information but some recommendations are:
-Create forums for dialogue for conflict prevention and host conflict resolution training
-Strengthen female leadership by enabling women to influence decisions at all levels: local, provincial and national. Encourage their participation in humanitarian and development mechanisms for equal opportunities.
-Changing socio-cultural constraintsand discriminatory customs through approaches such as Mobali pona Mwasi (men committed to women's rights)
-Implement functional literacy programmes to enable women and indigenous peoples to learn to read and write.
-Initiate training sessions on social entrepreneurship and the development of Income-Generating Activities (IGAs) for women, young people, albinos and indiginous populations.
-Supporting improved agriculture through robust approaches such as Champ École Paysan for better productivity and resilience.
-A project communication strategy was developed in consultation with partners, along with a project communication protocol and a work plan.
-Awareness-raising in the respective provinces. Based on a participatory approach, these sessions enabled the project to be presented to all stakeholders at the local, territorial and provincial levels in order to obtain their free, informed and prior consent (FIPC) before counting on their support and commitment in the implementation of the project. A total of eight awareness-raising sessions were organized in the four provinces, reaching a total of 221 beneficiaries, including 61 women (including women from indigenous peoples and local communities) and 160 men.
IMPACT has spent a lot of time strengthening financial management of partners. They organized an extra workshop in Lubumbashi in December 2024 to assure alignment of all partners with financial management, work procedures and implementation. This was a good adaptation. IMPACT informed the embassy before the change. Communication has throughout the first year been very good, IMPACT has been proactive and communicative. They have also showed professionalism in project management and in how they approach the project. It is noticable that they have a human centered approach, focus on inclusion and have clear procedures that they implement. They managed the challenging security situation that become worse in 2024 well. All studies and reports have been shared with the embassy. Sida is a new donor to IMPACT but IMPACT has been attentive and quickly adjusted to Sida standards when necessary. There were some delays in the start of the project due to some recrutment challenges but the project then picked up well and have been able to create a good starting point for year two and further implementation of activities.
The embassy did field visits in the same site in Haut Katanga in June 2024 and June 2025 and could confirm that communities have been organized and that the local partners were working as planned. The embassy also participated in training sessions for implemented partners in dec 2024 and in june 2025 and could confirm that IMPACT has a close collaboration and continuous support to local partners both with financial, communicative and technical skills. During the latest field visit in Katanga it was specifically discussed how the project can avoid creating new local structures if existing structures are available. In June 2025 embassy staff visited the Kolwezi office and in sep 2025 embassy staff visited the Bunia office. They were both well maintained, presented well their work and could answer questions. The office in Bunia had large maps of the project areas which made it easier to discuss implementation, it also had small test gardens where different plants were tested to see how they can later be implemented. It was clear that IMPACT have been working with the consortium a lot and experts traveling between provinces to educate and share experiences. In Bunia IMPACT staff rejected an invitation to a dinner with the embassy visitors since it was too late for them in the evening according to their security rules. This shows that the rules are respected, even when the donor sends an invitation.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
